issues.legal_issue: A landlord's genuine and honest need to use rented premises for a proposed business may be reasonable and bona fide even without dire necessity, loss of existing employment, completed business preparations, or prior business experience.
material_facts: The landlord's heir sought the premises to start a grocery business and said a workplace lock-out had made it difficult to support his family.
He had not resigned from his job, and the record did not establish that he had permanently lost it.
He had not proved that he had arranged capital, prepared to open the shop, or gained experience in grocery business.
The lower courts treated those matters, and the absence of dire necessity, as grounds to reject the claimed need.
issues.conclusion: The lower courts applied the wrong test. The heir's need to use the premises for a grocery business was not defeated by his continued employment, lack of completed preparations or experience, or failure to prove absolute necessity; eviction was ordered.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(1)(g) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1947 requires a reasonable and bona fide need. Reasonable requirement is an objective need between a mere wish and a compelling or absolute necessity; bona fides require an honest need without an oblique motive. A landlord need not reach starvation, resign an existing job, prove funds or completed preparations, or establish special expertise for an ordinary business. The Court relied on Bega Begum v. Abdul Ahad Khan, Mattulal v. Radhelal, Yudhishtir v. Ashok Kumar, A.K. Veeraraghava Iyengar v. N.V. Prasad, Vinay Kumar v. District Judge, Ghazipur, Rena Drego v. Lalchand Soni, Sarla Ahuja v. United India Insurance Co., Prativa Devi v. T.V. Krishnan, Meenal Eknath Kshirsagar v. Traders and Agencies, Sheela Chadha v. Accharaj Ram Sehgal, Shiv Sarup Gupta v. Mahesh Chand Gupta, and Raj Kumar Khaitan v. Bibi Zubaida Khatun.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking recovery of rented premises from a tenant.
predicates.landlord_seeks_premises_for_own_business: The landlord or a successor relying on the landlord's claim sought the premises to conduct a business there.
predicates.genuine_non_fanciful_need: The proposed use reflected an honest, genuine need rather than a mere wish or an oblique motive.

issues.definition: When a landlord in an eviction proceeding has an honest, genuine need to use the premises for a business, that need can qualify as reasonable and bona fide without being an absolute necessity.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may interfere with concurrent factual findings in a rent-control appeal when the lower courts' legally erroneous approach produces a manifestly unjust result.
material_facts: The trial court and appellate court both rejected the claimed need after treating dire necessity, permanent job loss, and business preparations as necessary proof.
The High Court declined to interfere because the findings were concurrent findings of fact.
The Supreme Court concluded that the lower courts had used the wrong legal test and relied on irrelevant considerations.
issues.conclusion: This was an exceptional case for interference under Article 136, and the concurrent decisions could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court ordinarily does not disturb findings of fact, but may do so in exceptional cases where concurrent decisions are manifestly unjust or rest on a substantial and patent error of law. The Court relied on Variety Emporium v. V.R.M. Mohd. Ibrahim Naina and Bega Begum v. Abdul Ahad Khan.

predicates.special_leave_appeal_from_concurrent_fin: A party brought a special-leave appeal challenging factual findings reached by more than one lower court.
predicates.lower_courts_used_wrong_legal_test: The lower courts assessed the claim using a legal test that did not govern the issue.
predicates.resulting_decision_manifestly_unjust: Applying the wrong test led to a manifestly unjust decision.

issues.definition: In a special-leave appeal, concurrent findings may be disturbed when the lower courts used the wrong legal test and that error produced a manifestly unjust decision.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant's late challenge to an amendment placing the heirs' own requirement in issue need not be entertained when both sides litigated that requirement and the amendment caused no prejudice.
material_facts: The original landlord died while the eviction suit was pending.
The heirs obtained an amendment pleading one heir's own need to use the premises for a grocery business.
Both sides then presented evidence on the amended claim, and the tenant had a full opportunity to meet it.
The proceedings had continued for years, and the Supreme Court found no prejudice to the tenant from the amendment.
The tenant argued that the amendment had been wrongly allowed and that the heirs should have to file a fresh suit.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined, in its discretion under Article 136, to entertain the objection to the amendment or require the heirs to bring a fresh suit.
issues.legal_principle: Phool Rani v. Naubat Rai Ahluwalia was relied on for the contention that a deceased landlord's personal need could cease and that the heirs' need could differ. Shantilal Thakordas v. C.M. Telwala overruled Phool Rani on the main point, holding that a claim for the landlord's need and that of family members could continue through the heirs. In this case, because an amendment expressly raised the heirs' own requirement, both sides had litigated it, and the tenant suffered no prejudice, the Court exercised its discretion under Article 136 not to entertain the late objection. Order 6 Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure was the provision under which the amendment had been sought and allowed.

rule.if: eviction_suit_continued_by_heirs_after_landlord_death and amendment_put_heirs_own_need_in_issue and both_sides_litigated_amended_need and tenant_had_full_opportunity and no_prejudice_from_amendment

predicates.eviction_suit_continued_by_heirs_after_l: After the landlord died during an eviction suit, the heirs continued the proceeding.
predicates.amendment_put_heirs_own_need_in_issue: The heirs obtained an amendment raising their own need for the premises.
predicates.both_sides_litigated_amended_need: Both sides presented evidence and litigated the need raised by the amendment.
predicates.tenant_had_full_opportunity: The tenant had a full opportunity to meet the amended claim.
predicates.no_prejudice_from_amendment: The amendment caused no prejudice to the tenant.

issues.definition: When heirs continue an eviction suit after the landlord's death, amend it to raise their own need, and litigate that need with no prejudice to a tenant who had a full opportunity to respond, a late objection to the amendment need not be entertained.
